questions.sec: Thyrotoxicosis: clinical features and Graves disease
questions.q: Match the following thyrotoxic features to their system — 1) Weight loss, heat intolerance 2) Tremor, hyperreflexia 3) Atrial fibrillation 4) Diarrhoea … A) Constitutional B) Neurological C) Cardiovascular D) Gastrointestinal
questions.exp: Constitutional (weight loss, heat intolerance), neurological (tremor, hyperreflexia), cardiovascular (AF) and gastrointestinal (diarrhoea) are the four feature groups on the page. (Book p910)

questions.sec: Thyrotoxicosis: clinical features and Graves disease
questions.q: A 35-year-old woman has weight loss, palpitations, lid lag and a diffuse goitre with bruit. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.exp: Diffuse goitre with bruit, ophthalmopathy and young female demographic fits Graves disease. (Book p910)

questions.sec: Thyrotoxicosis: clinical features and Graves disease
questions.q: Assess these thyrotoxic features: I Sinus tachycardia is the most common rhythm. II Atrial fibrillation occurs in a minority of younger patients.
questions.exp: Sinus tachycardia is most common; atrial fibrillation occurs in older patients rather than the young. (Book p910)

questions.sec: Thyrotoxicosis: clinical features and Graves disease
questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a feature of thyrotoxicosis NOT shared with anxiety?
opts: Suppressed TSH with raised free T4
questions.exp: Biochemical suppression of TSH with raised free T4 is specific to thyrotoxicosis; tremor, palpitations and weight loss overlap with anxiety. (Book p910)

questions.sec: Thyrotoxicosis: clinical features and Graves disease
questions.q: The single most specific clinical sign of Graves disease listed on the page is ___.
questions.exp: Infiltrative ophthalmopathy is Graves-specific; sinus tachycardia, tremor and diffuse goitre also occur in other causes. (Book p910)

questions.sec: Thyrotoxicosis: clinical features and Graves disease
questions.q: Match the following Graves feature — 1) Eye signs 2) Skin signs 3) Skeletal signs … A) Exophthalmos, proptosis B) Pretibial myxoedema C) Thyroid acropachy
questions.exp: Graves-specific manifestations include exophthalmos (eye), pretibial myxoedema (skin) and thyroid acropachy (skeletal). (Book p910)

questions.sec: Thyrotoxicosis: clinical features and Graves disease
questions.q: A patient with Graves disease has non-pitting oedema with peau d'orange over the shins. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Pretibial myxoedema is a Graves-specific dermopathy producing non-pitting oedema with peau d'orange over the shins. (Book p910)

questions.sec: Thyrotoxicosis: clinical features and Graves disease
questions.q: Assess Graves extra-thyroidal manifestations: I Thyroid acropachy affects the distal phalanges. II Pretibial myxoedema can occur even after euthyroidism is restored.
questions.exp: Acropachy is a clubbing-like change of distal phalanges; dermopathy can persist or even appear after euthyroidism. (Book p910)

questions.sec: Thyrotoxicosis: clinical features and Graves disease
questions.q: Match the following finding to its likely cause in a thyrotoxic patient — 1) Diffuse goitre with bruit 2) Painful tender thyroid 3) Single hot nodule on scan 4) Multiple hot nodules … A) Graves disease B) Subacute thyroiditis C) Toxic adenoma D) Toxic multinodular goitre
questions.exp: Graves shows a diffuse goitre with bruit; subacute thyroiditis is painful and tender; a single hot nodule is a toxic adenoma; multiple hot nodules fit toxic MNG. (Book p910)

questions.sec: Thyrotoxicosis: clinical features and Graves disease
questions.q: A 50-year-old woman has a long-standing multinodular goitre and new atrial fibrillation with weight loss. The most likely aetiology is:
questions.exp: Long-standing MNG degenerating into toxic MNG is the typical aetiology in older women with new AF and weight loss. (Book p910)

questions.sec: Thyrotoxicosis: clinical features and Graves disease
questions.q: Which extra-thyroidal manifestation is unique to Graves disease among all causes of thyrotoxicosis?
questions.exp: Infiltrative ophthalmopathy is Graves-specific; other features occur in any thyrotoxicosis. (Book p910)

questions.sec: Thyrotoxicosis: clinical features and Graves disease
questions.q: The radioactive iodine uptake scan in Graves disease typically shows ___ uptake.
opts: Focally increased in a single nodule
questions.exp: Graves produces diffusely increased uptake; toxic adenoma is focal; toxic MNG is multiple focal; thyroiditis is decreased. (Book p910)

questions.sec: Thyrotoxicosis: clinical features and Graves disease
questions.q: Assess the page's eye-signs grouping: I Proptosis and chemosis are Graves-specific. II Lid lag and lid retraction can occur in any thyrotoxicosis.
questions.exp: Infiltrative eye signs are Graves-specific; lid lag and lid retraction occur in any thyrotoxicosis because of sympathetic overactivity. (Book p910)

questions.sec: Graves eye signs, scoring and diagnosis
questions.q: Match the following Graves eye sign to its description — 1) Proptosis 2) Chemosis 3) Diplopia 4) Lid lag … A) Forward displacement of the globe B) Conjunctival oedema C) Restricted extraocular motility D) Lid fails to follow eye on downward gaze
questions.exp: Proptosis is forward globe displacement; chemosis is conjunctival oedema; diplopia is from restrictive myopathy and motility restriction; lid lag is failure to follow downward gaze. (Book p911)

questions.sec: Graves eye signs, scoring and diagnosis
questions.q: A patient with Graves disease has red, swollen conjunctiva and restricted eye movements bilaterally. The activity score category is most consistent with:
questions.exp: Conjunctival redness and oedema with restrictive motility denote active moderate-to-severe Graves ophthalmopathy. (Book p911)

questions.sec: Graves eye signs, scoring and diagnosis
questions.q: Assess Graves ophthalmopathy: I Smoking dramatically worsens the course. II Radioiodine therapy can worsen eye disease in active ophthalmopathy.
questions.exp: Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for progression; radioiodine can transiently worsen active ophthalmopathy. (Book p911)

questions.sec: Graves eye signs, scoring and diagnosis
questions.q: Which is the odd one out — an inactive Graves ophthalmopathy feature?
questions.exp: Recent deterioration in diplopia suggests active disease; long-standing proptosis, stable lid lag and fibrotic restrictive strabismus denote inactive disease. (Book p911)

questions.sec: Graves eye signs, scoring and diagnosis
questions.q: The single most important modifiable risk factor for progression of Graves ophthalmopathy is ___.
questions.exp: Smoking cessation is the strongest modifiable intervention; radioiodine should be avoided or covered with steroids in active disease. (Book p911)

questions.sec: Graves eye signs, scoring and diagnosis
questions.q: Match the following Graves investigation to its expected finding — 1) TSH-receptor antibody 2) Anti-TPO 3) Thyroid uptake scan 4) Orbital MRI … A) Positive in most untreated Graves B) Often positive (less specific) C) Diffusely increased uptake D) Enlarged extraocular muscles
questions.exp: TRAb is positive in most untreated Graves; anti-TPO is often present but less specific; uptake scan shows diffuse increase; orbital MRI shows enlarged muscle bellies. (Book p911)

questions.sec: Graves eye signs, scoring and diagnosis
questions.q: A 40-year-old woman has new thyrotoxicosis, positive TRAb and bilateral proptosis. The most consistent diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Positive TRAb with bilateral proptosis and thyrotoxicosis is diagnostic of Graves disease. (Book p911)

questions.sec: Graves eye signs, scoring and diagnosis
questions.q: Assess the differential: I Hashitoxicosis can mimic Graves initially. II Toxic adenoma typically has negative TRAb.
questions.exp: Hashitoxicosis is a transient Graves-like picture early in Hashimoto disease; toxic adenoma is a focal hot nodule with negative TRAb. (Book p911)

questions.sec: Graves eye signs, scoring and diagnosis
questions.q: Match the following clinical clue to the diagnosis — 1) Painful thyroid with elevated ESR 2) Diffuse goitre with bruit 3) Single hot nodule on scan 4) Recent amiodarone use with low uptake … A) Subacute thyroiditis B) Graves disease C) Toxic adenoma D) Type 2 amiodarone thyrotoxicosis
questions.exp: Painful thyroid with raised ESR is subacute thyroiditis; diffuse goitre with bruit is Graves; a single hot nodule is toxic adenoma; amiodarone with low uptake is Type 2 destructive thyroiditis. (Book p911)

questions.sec: Graves eye signs, scoring and diagnosis
questions.q: An older patient with atrial fibrillation and new weight loss has a thyroid scan with multiple focal hot areas. The best diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Multiple focal hot areas in an older patient fit toxic MNG; Graves would be diffusely increased. (Book p911)

questions.sec: Graves eye signs, scoring and diagnosis
questions.q: The radioactive iodine uptake pattern in toxic adenoma is ___.
opts: Focally increased in the nodule with suppressed surrounding gland
questions.exp: Toxic adenoma shows a focal hot area with suppressed extranodular tissue; toxic MNG shows multiple focal hot areas. (Book p911)

questions.sec: Graves eye signs, scoring and diagnosis
questions.q: Assess eye-disease management: I High-dose glucocorticoids are first-line for active moderate-to-severe disease. II Orbital radiotherapy is reserved for active disease failing steroids.
questions.exp: IV methylprednisolone is first-line for active moderate-to-severe Graves ophthalmopathy; orbital radiotherapy is an option for active disease not controlled by steroids. (Book p911)

questions.sec: Thionamides, RAI and surgical management of thyrotoxicosis
questions.q: Match the following thionamide feature — 1) Methimazole 2) Propylthiouracil 3) Carbimazole 4) Block-and-replace regimen … A) Preferred in most adults B) Preferred in T1 pregnancy and thyroid storm C) Prodrug of methimazole D) Thionamide + levothyroxine combination
questions.exp: Methimazole is preferred in non-pregnant adults; PTU is reserved for T1 pregnancy and thyroid storm; carbimazole is the prodrug of methimazole; block-and-replace is a thionamide-plus-levothyroxine combination. (Book p912)

questions.sec: Thionamides, RAI and surgical management of thyrotoxicosis
questions.q: A woman in the first trimester of pregnancy needs treatment for Graves disease. Which thionamide is the most appropriate?
questions.exp: PTU is preferred in T1 because methimazole is associated with embryopathy; methimazole is preferred from T2 onward. (Book p912)

questions.sec: Thionamides, RAI and surgical management of thyrotoxicosis
questions.q: Assess thionamide adverse effects: I Agranulocytosis is a rare but serious idiosyncratic reaction. II Methimazole carries a black-box warning for hepatotoxicity in T1 pregnancy.
questions.exp: Agranulocytosis is a rare idiosyncratic reaction with both thionamides; PTU carries the hepatotoxicity warning (especially in T1 pregnancy), not methimazole. (Book p912)

questions.sec: Thionamides, RAI and surgical management of thyrotoxicosis
questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a side-effect not typical of methimazole?
questions.exp: Severe hepatotoxicity with hepatic failure is the PTU-type pattern; methimazole typically causes cholestatic liver enzyme rise, not severe hepatotoxicity. (Book p912)

questions.sec: Thionamides, RAI and surgical management of thyrotoxicosis
questions.q: The thionamide dose in Graves disease is adjusted aiming for ___.
opts: Free T4 / free T3 normalisation before TSH recovery
questions.exp: Free T4/T3 normalise earlier than TSH; dose is titrated to free hormones with TSH as a delayed check. (Book p912)

questions.sec: Thionamides, RAI and surgical management of thyrotoxicosis
questions.q: Match the following definitive therapy — 1) Radioactive iodine ablation 2) Total thyroidectomy 3) Antithyroid drugs … A) Definitive in selected patients with low ophthalmopathy risk B) Rapid control in pregnancy and large goitres C) Long-term remission in ~50% of Graves patients
questions.exp: RAI is definitive when eye disease is inactive; surgery is preferred in pregnancy with large goitres or rapid control; thionamides achieve long-term remission in about half of patients. (Book p912)

questions.sec: Thionamides, RAI and surgical management of thyrotoxicosis
questions.q: A patient with Graves disease has active moderate ophthalmopathy and a large goitre. Which definitive therapy is most appropriate?
questions.exp: Active ophthalmopathy and large goitre favour thyroidectomy; RAI should be covered with steroids in active eye disease. (Book p912)

questions.sec: Thionamides, RAI and surgical management of thyrotoxicosis
questions.q: Assess RAI: I It is contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding. II It can cause thyroiditis and transient thyrotoxicosis.
questions.exp: RAI is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding; post-RAI thyroiditis can cause transient thyrotoxicosis before hypothyroidism. (Book p912)

questions.sec: Thionamides, RAI and surgical management of thyrotoxicosis
questions.q: Match the following adjunct — 1) Beta-blocker 2) NSAID 3) Calcium supplementation 4) Cholestyramine … A) Symptomatic control of adrenergic symptoms B) Analgesia in subacute thyroiditis C) Bone protection in chronic thyrotoxicosis D) Reduces enterohepatic recycling of thyroid hormone
questions.exp: Beta-blockers control adrenergic symptoms; NSAIDs are analgesics in subacute thyroiditis; calcium supports bone in chronic thyrotoxicosis; cholestyramine reduces enterohepatic recycling of thyroid hormone. (Book p912)

questions.sec: Thionamides, RAI and surgical management of thyrotoxicosis
questions.q: A patient on methimazole develops sore throat and fever; total neutrophil count is 0.4 × 10⁹/L. The next step is:
opts: Add lithium to boost white cells (alternative)
Stop methimazole immediately and admit for neutropenic sepsis work-up
Continue methimazole and add G-CSF as outpatient
questions.exp: Agranulocytosis requires immediate cessation of the thionamide and urgent management of neutropenic sepsis risk. (Book p912)

questions.sec: Thionamides, RAI and surgical management of thyrotoxicosis
questions.q: The block-and-replace regimen pairs a thionamide with ___ to avoid hypothyroidism.
questions.exp: Block-and-replace uses a fixed thionamide dose plus levothyroxine to maintain euthyroidism during the block. (Book p912)

questions.sec: Thionamides, RAI and surgical management of thyrotoxicosis
questions.q: Assess treatment duration: I Antithyroid drug course is typically 12–18 months. II Most Graves patients achieve permanent remission with thionamides alone.
questions.exp: A typical course is 12–18 months; permanent remission occurs in roughly half of patients, not most. (Book p912)

questions.sec: Thyroid storm, neonatal thyrotoxicosis, surgery complications
questions.q: Match the following thyroid-storm feature — 1) Trigger 2) Burch-Wartofsky component 3) First-line thionamide 4) Adjunct … A) Infection / surgery / trauma B) Score ≥ 45 suggests storm C) Propylthiouracil D) Iodine (≥1 h after thionamide) + beta-blocker + steroid
questions.exp: Triggers include infection, surgery and trauma; Burch-Wartofsky ≥ 45 suggests storm; PTU is preferred in storm; iodine is given at least one hour after thionamide along with beta-blocker and steroid. (Book p913)

questions.sec: Thyroid storm, neonatal thyrotoxicosis, surgery complications
questions.q: A patient with Graves disease post-appendicectomy has fever 39.5 °C, HR 158/min, agitation and jaundice. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: High fever, tachyarrhythmia, agitation and jaundice after a precipitating event in Graves fit thyroid storm. (Book p913)

questions.sec: Thyroid storm, neonatal thyrotoxicosis, surgery complications
questions.q: Assess thyroid storm management: I Iodine should precede the thionamide. II IV hydrocortisone is part of the regimen.
questions.exp: Iodine is given at least one hour after the thionamide to avoid substrate for new hormone; hydrocortisone covers possible adrenal insufficiency and reduces T4-to-T3 conversion. (Book p913)

questions.sec: Thyroid storm, neonatal thyrotoxicosis, surgery complications
questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a treatment used in thyroid storm?
questions.exp: PTU, propranolol and hydrocortisone are standard; lithium is not standard storm therapy (it can be adjunct in severe cases but not routine). (Book p913)

questions.sec: Thyroid storm, neonatal thyrotoxicosis, surgery complications
questions.q: The Burch-Wartofsky score ≥ ___ suggests thyroid storm.
questions.exp: A score of 45 or more on the Burch-Wartofsky scale is highly suggestive of thyroid storm. (Book p913)

questions.sec: Thyroid storm, neonatal thyrotoxicosis, surgery complications
questions.q: Match the following context — 1) Neonatal thyrotoxicosis 2) Postpartum Graves 3) Subclinical thyrotoxicosis 4) Apathetic thyrotoxicosis … A) Transplacental TRAb; treat with thionamide B) May flare after delivery C) TSH < 0.1 with normal free hormones D) Elderly with apathy rather than hyperactivity
questions.exp: Neonatal thyrotoxicosis is from transplacental TRAb; postpartum Graves may flare after delivery; subclinical thyrotoxicosis has low TSH with normal free hormones; apathetic thyrotoxicosis presents with apathy in elderly. (Book p913)

questions.sec: Thyroid storm, neonatal thyrotoxicosis, surgery complications
questions.q: A neonate born to a mother with active Graves disease has tachycardia, irritability and poor weight gain. The most appropriate therapy is:
questions.exp: Neonatal thyrotoxicosis is treated with thionamide (methimazole preferred after first weeks) plus a beta-blocker; iodide can be added. (Book p913)

questions.sec: Thyroid storm, neonatal thyrotoxicosis, surgery complications
questions.q: Assess neonatal thyrotoxicosis: I It is caused by transplacental TSH-receptor antibodies. II It typically resolves as maternal antibodies clear over weeks.
questions.exp: Maternal TRAb crosses the placenta; symptoms resolve over weeks to months as antibodies wane. (Book p913)

questions.sec: Thyroid storm, neonatal thyrotoxicosis, surgery complications
questions.q: Match the following surgical complication of thyroidectomy — 1) Hypoparathyroidism 2) Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury 3) Haematoma with airway compromise 4) Hypothyroidism … A) Hypocalcaemia with tetany B) Hoarseness / stridor C) Emergency airway decompression D) Expected after total thyroidectomy
questions.exp: Hypoparathyroidism causes hypocalcaemia and tetany; recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes hoarseness or stridor; neck haematoma is an airway emergency; hypothyroidism is expected after total thyroidectomy. (Book p913)

questions.sec: Thyroid storm, neonatal thyrotoxicosis, surgery complications
questions.q: A patient has stridor and a tense neck haematoma within hours of thyroidectomy. The next step is:
opts: CT scan of the neck before intervention
Emergency wound decompression at the bedside
questions.exp: Post-thyroidectomy haematoma with airway compromise requires immediate opening of the wound at the bedside before definitive airway. (Book p913)

questions.sec: Thyroid storm, neonatal thyrotoxicosis, surgery complications
questions.q: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury post-thyroidectomy can cause ___.
opts: Bilateral vocal-cord paralysis and airway obstruction
questions.exp: Bilateral injury causes vocal-cord paralysis in the adducted position and acute airway obstruction requiring tracheostomy. (Book p913)

questions.sec: Thyroid storm, neonatal thyrotoxicosis, surgery complications
questions.q: Assess surgery in Graves: I Total thyroidectomy achieves rapid control. II It is preferred in patients with active moderate ophthalmopathy.
questions.exp: Total thyroidectomy rapidly controls hyperthyroidism and is preferred in active ophthalmopathy to avoid RAI-induced flare. (Book p913)

questions.sec: Thyroiditis classification
questions.q: Match the following thyroiditis to its feature — 1) Hashimoto 2) Subacute (de Quervain) 3) Postpartum 4) Acute suppurative … A) Painless firm goitre with anti-TPO B) Painful tender thyroid with raised ESR C) Within 12 months of delivery D) Bacterial, painful, requires drainage
questions.exp: Hashimoto presents with painless firm goitre and high anti-TPO; subacute thyroiditis is painful with raised ESR; postpartum thyroiditis occurs within 12 months of delivery; acute suppurative thyroiditis is bacterial and needs drainage. (Book p914)

questions.sec: Thyroiditis classification
questions.q: A 28-year-old woman 5 months postpartum has painless thyroid enlargement with suppressed TSH and raised anti-TPO. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Painless thyroid dysfunction within 12 months of delivery with positive anti-TPO fits postpartum thyroiditis. (Book p914)

questions.sec: Thyroiditis classification
questions.q: Assess postpartum thyroiditis: I It typically follows a thyrotoxic then hypothyroid course. II It is usually self-limiting.
questions.exp: Postpartum thyroiditis often biphasic (toxic → hypo) and resolves within 12–18 months; some patients progress to permanent hypothyroidism. (Book p914)

questions.sec: Thyroiditis classification
questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a feature distinguishing subacute thyroiditis from Graves?
questions.exp: Painless diffuse goitre with bruit is Graves; tenderness, very high ESR and low uptake are subacute thyroiditis. (Book p914)

questions.sec: Thyroiditis classification
questions.q: The classic viral prodrome and painful thyroid of subacute thyroiditis is treated symptomatically with ___.
questions.exp: Subacute thyroiditis is treated with NSAIDs for pain and beta-blocker for thyrotoxic symptoms; thionamides are not effective. (Book p914)

questions.sec: Thyroiditis classification
questions.q: Match the following thyroiditis to its uptake scan — 1) Hashimoto 2) Subacute 3) Postpartum 4) Acute suppurative … A) Variable B) Low uptake C) Low uptake D) Low uptake (cold abscess)
questions.exp: Hashimoto uptake is variable; subacute, postpartum and acute suppurative thyroiditis all show low uptake due to glandular destruction. (Book p914)

questions.sec: Thyroiditis classification
questions.q: A 35-year-old has neck pain, fever 38.5 °C and a tender thyroid with ESR 90 mm/h one week after a viral URI. The most consistent diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Painful tender thyroid with high ESR after a viral illness fits subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis. (Book p914)

questions.sec: Thyroiditis classification
questions.q: Assess thyroiditis treatment: I Antithyroid drugs are first-line for subacute thyroiditis. II NSAIDs are effective for the pain of subacute thyroiditis.
questions.exp: NSAIDs (and corticosteroids in severe cases) manage pain; thionamides are not effective because hormone is released, not synthesised. (Book p914)

questions.sec: Thyroiditis classification
questions.q: Match the following thyroiditis to the preferred treatment — 1) Subacute 2) Postpartum 3) Acute suppurative 4) Hashimoto with hypothyroidism … A) NSAIDs + beta-blocker B) Beta-blocker ± levothyroxine C) IV antibiotics + drainage D) Levothyroxine replacement
questions.exp: Subacute thyroiditis uses NSAIDs and beta-blocker; postpartum thyroiditis is supportive with beta-blocker and levothyroxine in the hypothyroid phase; acute suppurative thyroiditis needs IV antibiotics and drainage; hypothyroid Hashimoto needs levothyroxine. (Book p914)

questions.sec: Thyroiditis classification
questions.q: A patient has fever, severe neck pain and fluctuant thyroid swelling with overlying erythema. The most appropriate next step is:
questions.exp: Acute suppurative thyroiditis is a surgical infection requiring IV antibiotics and drainage. (Book p914)

questions.sec: Thyroiditis classification
questions.q: Postpartum thyroiditis occurs within ___ months of delivery.
questions.exp: Postpartum thyroiditis is defined within 12 months of delivery, often biphasic with recovery over 12–18 months. (Book p914)

questions.sec: Thyroiditis classification
questions.q: Assess thyroiditis associations: I Subacute thyroiditis may follow mumps, measles or coxsackievirus. II Painless thyroiditis is typically postpartum.
questions.exp: Subacute thyroiditis is associated with viral infections; painless thyroiditis typically refers to postpartum and silent variants. (Book p914)

questions.sec: Subacute and postpartum thyroiditis course
questions.q: Match the following thyroiditis phase to its expected TFT pattern — 1) Hyperthyroid phase 2) Hypothyroid phase 3) Recovery … A) ↑FT4, ↓TSH, low uptake, raised ESR B) ↓FT4, ↑TSH, low uptake C) Normal TFTs and ESR
questions.exp: Hyperthyroid phase has high free T4/T3 with low TSH and raised ESR; hypothyroid phase has low free hormone with high TSH; recovery normalises both TFTs and ESR. (Book p915)

questions.sec: Subacute and postpartum thyroiditis course
questions.q: An outpatient with subacute thyroiditis at week 6 still has fatigue, weight gain and a TSH of 12 mIU/L. The most appropriate therapy is:
opts: Levothyroxine replacement during the hypothyroid phase
questions.exp: The hypothyroid phase is treated with levothyroxine; thionamides are ineffective because hormone is not being synthesised. (Book p915)

questions.sec: Subacute and postpartum thyroiditis course
questions.q: Assess postpartum thyroiditis: I Anti-TPO antibodies predict higher risk. II Permanent hypothyroidism develops in a minority.
questions.exp: Anti-TPO positivity predicts postpartum thyroiditis; permanent hypothyroidism develops in roughly 20–30% of affected women. (Book p915)

questions.sec: Subacute and postpartum thyroiditis course
questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a feature of subacute thyroiditis (de Quervain)?
opts: Diffuse painless goitre without ESR rise
questions.exp: Painless goitre without ESR rise fits painless/postpartum thyroiditis rather than the painful de Quervain subacute variant. (Book p915)

questions.sec: Subacute and postpartum thyroiditis course
questions.q: Pain in subacute thyroiditis typically responds to ___; corticosteroids are reserved for severe cases.
questions.exp: NSAIDs are first-line analgesia; corticosteroids are added in severe or refractory cases. (Book p915)

questions.sec: Subacute and postpartum thyroiditis course
questions.q: Match the following graph feature — 1) X-axis 2) Y-axes (left/right) 3) Toxic phase timing … A) Time (weeks from onset) B) UT4 (left) and ESR (right) C) Weeks 0–4 typically thyrotoxic
questions.exp: The schematic plots time in weeks on the x-axis; UT4 (free T4) and ESR appear on the y-axes; the toxic phase occupies weeks 0–4 of illness. (Book p915)

questions.sec: Subacute and postpartum thyroiditis course
questions.q: At week 8 of subacute thyroiditis, the patient has normal free T4 and normal ESR. The best next step is:
opts: Continue to monitor with periodic TFTs
questions.exp: Recovery normalises TFTs and ESR; further observation without specific therapy is appropriate, with follow-up for late hypothyroidism. (Book p915)

questions.sec: Subacute and postpartum thyroiditis course
questions.q: Assess these statements: I Corticosteroids shorten painful phase but do not prevent hypothyroidism. II Subacute thyroiditis always recurs.
questions.exp: Corticosteroids ease symptoms without altering the natural biphasic course; recurrence is uncommon though possible. (Book p915)

questions.sec: Subacute and postpartum thyroiditis course
questions.q: Match the following postpartum thyroiditis finding to its prevalence — 1) Anti-TPO positive 2) Symptomatic thyroid dysfunction 3) Permanent hypothyroidism … A) ~50% of women who develop it B) Up to 5–10% of pregnancies C) ~20–30% of cases
questions.exp: Among women with postpartum thyroiditis, about half are anti-TPO positive; symptomatic disease occurs in 5–10% of pregnancies; permanent hypothyroidism develops in ~20–30% of cases. (Book p915)

questions.sec: Subacute and postpartum thyroiditis course
questions.q: A 32-year-old with postpartum thyroiditis asks about future pregnancies. Which statement is most consistent with the source?
opts: Recurrence risk is high in subsequent pregnancies
questions.exp: Recurrence in subsequent pregnancies is common; permanent hypothyroidism is possible but not inevitable. (Book p915)

questions.sec: Subacute and postpartum thyroiditis course
questions.q: Recurrent subacute thyroiditis occurs in roughly ___% of patients.
questions.exp: Recurrence after de Quervain thyroiditis is uncommon, around 1–4% in published series; the page emphasises the typically self-limiting nature. (Book p915)

questions.sec: Subacute and postpartum thyroiditis course
questions.q: Assess these caveats: I Postpartum thyroiditis can be mistaken for Graves disease initially. II Both disorders show low uptake on scan.
questions.exp: Postpartum thyroiditis can mimic Graves early, but Graves shows high uptake whereas postpartum thyroiditis shows low uptake. (Book p915)

questions.sec: Amiodarone thyroid disease and drug-induced thyroiditis
questions.q: Match the following amiodarone thyroid pattern — 1) Type 1 2) Type 2 3) Euthyroid 4) Subclinical hypothyroidism on amiodarone … A) Iodine-induced hyperthyroidism B) Destructive thyroiditis C) Hormone release with normal TFTs D) Mildly raised TSH, normal free T4
questions.exp: Type 1 is iodine-induced hyperthyroidism in predisposed glands; Type 2 is destructive thyroiditis with low uptake; many patients remain euthyroid; subclinical hypothyroidism can occur especially in iodine-replete regions. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone thyroid disease and drug-induced thyroiditis
questions.q: A cardiac patient on amiodarone develops weight loss with suppressed TSH and very low uptake on scan. The most consistent diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Low uptake on scan in an amiodarone-treated patient fits destructive (Type 2) thyrotoxicosis; Type 1 has preserved or increased uptake. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone thyroid disease and drug-induced thyroiditis
questions.q: Assess amiodarone thyroid disease: I Type 1 occurs in abnormal glands (nodules or latent Graves). II Type 2 occurs in normal glands via destructive thyroiditis.
questions.exp: Type 1 typically requires underlying nodular or autoimmune disease; Type 2 occurs even in normal glands because of direct toxicity and release of preformed hormone. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone thyroid disease and drug-induced thyroiditis
questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a treatment for Type 2 amiodarone thyrotoxicosis?
opts: Thyroidectomy if severe and amiodarone cannot be stopped
questions.exp: Type 2 responds to corticosteroids; thionamides are largely ineffective in destructive thyroiditis, making them the odd one out for first-line use. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone thyroid disease and drug-induced thyroiditis
questions.q: The half-life of amiodarone and its iodine load means amiodarone thyroid disease can develop up to ___ after stopping therapy.
questions.exp: Amiodarone's long half-life (50–100 days) and iodine load mean thyroid disease can occur or persist for many months after discontinuation. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone thyroid disease and drug-induced thyroiditis
questions.q: Match the following drug to its thyroid effect — 1) Lithium 2) Interferon-α 3) Immune checkpoint inhibitors 4) Amiodarone … A) Inhibits hormone release B) Often reversible thyroiditis C) Can cause thyroiditis / hypo- or hyperthyroidism D) Both hypothyroidism and thyrotoxicosis via iodine load
questions.exp: Lithium inhibits hormone release; IFN-α commonly causes reversible thyroiditis; ICIs can cause thyroiditis with hypo- or hyperthyroidism; amiodarone causes both via its iodine load. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone thyroid disease and drug-induced thyroiditis
questions.q: A patient on pembrolizumab develops new atrial fibrillation with suppressed TSH and a low uptake scan. The next best diagnostic step is:
opts: Diagnose ICI-induced thyroiditis and treat with beta-blocker ± steroids
questions.exp: ICI-induced thyroiditis typically presents as thyrotoxicosis with low uptake; treat with beta-blocker and steroids if severe. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone thyroid disease and drug-induced thyroiditis
questions.q: Assess ICI thyroid toxicity: I Hypothyroidism often follows the thyrotoxic phase. II ICIs never cause Graves-like disease.
questions.exp: ICI-induced biphasic thyroiditis is common, with hypothyroid phase following the thyrotoxic phase; rare Graves-like disease is reported but unusual. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone thyroid disease and drug-induced thyroiditis
questions.q: Match the following diagnostic clue — 1) IL-6 elevation 2) High uptake with vascular nodule 3) Preserved uptake in iodine-replete gland 4) Anti-TPO and anti-Tg antibodies … A) Type 2 amiodarone thyrotoxicosis B) Type 1 amiodarone thyrotoxicosis C) Autoimmune predisposition D) Hashimoto thyroiditis
questions.exp: IL-6 rise supports Type 2 destructive thyroiditis; high uptake with a vascular nodule fits Type 1; preserved uptake in iodine-replete gland suggests an autoimmune predisposition; anti-TPO/Tg point to Hashimoto. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone thyroid disease and drug-induced thyroiditis
questions.q: A 65-year-old on amiodarone for AF develops overt hypothyroidism; the cardiac team is unwilling to stop amiodarone. The most consistent therapy is:
questions.exp: Amiodarone-induced hypothyroidism is treated with levothyroxine; amiodarone is continued if needed for cardiac control. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone thyroid disease and drug-induced thyroiditis
questions.q: Amiodarone contains approximately ___ mg of iodine per 200 mg tablet (each tablet carries a large iodine load).
questions.exp: Each 200 mg tablet of amiodarone contains about 75 mg of iodine; this massive iodine load is the basis of its thyroid effects. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone thyroid disease and drug-induced thyroiditis
questions.q: Assess amiodarone's iodine: I Daily iodine release greatly exceeds the WHO recommended intake. II Iodine excess can transiently inhibit organification (Wolff-Chaikoff effect).
questions.exp: Amiodarone releases ~7 mg of iodine daily, far above WHO recommendations; Wolff-Chaikoff effect describes transient inhibition of organification by iodine excess. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone thyroid disease and drug-induced thyroiditis
questions.q: Which is the odd one out among drugs listed as causing thyroiditis?
questions.exp: Levothyroxine is replacement therapy, not a cause of thyroiditis; IFN-α, ICIs and amiodarone are recognised triggers. (Book p916)

units.title: Thyrotoxicosis: clinical features and Graves disease
units.sec: Thyrotoxicosis: clinical features and Graves disease · p910
units.guide: Map constitutional, neurological, cardiovascular and gastrointestinal features of thyrotoxicosis. Recognise infiltrative ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxoedema and acropachy as Graves-specific.

units.title: Graves eye signs, scoring and diagnosis
units.sec: Graves eye signs, scoring and diagnosis · p911
units.guide: Use activity and severity scoring to classify Graves ophthalmopathy. Smoking cessation and steroid cover for radioiodine are central to management; TRAb positivity separates Graves from most mimics.

units.title: Thionamides, RAI and surgical management of thyrotoxicosis
units.sec: Thionamides, RAI and surgical management of thyrotoxicosis · p912
units.guide: Methimazole is preferred in non-pregnant adults; PTU is reserved for T1 pregnancy and thyroid storm. RAI is definitive but avoided in active ophthalmopathy; total thyroidectomy is preferred in large goitres and pregnancy.

units.title: Thyroid storm, neonatal thyrotoxicosis, surgery complications
units.sec: Thyroid storm, neonatal thyrotoxicosis, surgery complications · p913
units.guide: Burch-Wartofsky ≥ 45 suggests thyroid storm; treat with thionamide first, iodine after ≥1 h, beta-blocker and hydrocortisone. Neonatal thyrotoxicosis from transplacental TRAb is treated with thionamide plus beta-blocker.

units.title: Thyroiditis classification
units.guide: Distinguish Hashimoto, subacute (de Quervain), postpartum and acute suppurative thyroiditis by pain, ESR, antibodies and uptake. NSAID and beta-blocker treat subacute; antibiotics and drainage treat acute suppurative.

units.title: Subacute and postpartum thyroiditis course
units.sec: Subacute and postpartum thyroiditis course · p915
units.guide: Subacute and postpartum thyroiditis follow a biphasic course with eventual recovery in most patients. NSAIDs ease pain; levothyroxine covers the hypothyroid phase; permanent hypothyroidism develops in a minority.

units.title: Amiodarone thyroid disease and drug-induced thyroiditis
units.sec: Amiodarone thyroid disease and drug-induced thyroiditis · p916
units.guide: Type 1 amiodarone thyrotoxicosis is iodine-induced (treated with thionamides); Type 2 is destructive (treated with steroids). Lithium, IFN-α and ICIs each have characteristic thyroid signatures worth memorising.
